etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English seryows, from Old French serieux, from Medieval Latin sēriōsus, an extension of Latin sērius (“grave, earnest, serious”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy”). Cognate with German schwer (“heavy, difficult, severe”), Old English swǣr (“heavy, grave, grievous”). More at swear, sweer.

definitions.definition: Without humor or expression of happiness; grave in manner or disposition
Really intending what is said (or planned, etc); in earnest; not jocular or deceiving
(colloquial or dialect) seriously, in a serious manner (most often heard in take or mean serious)

quote.citation: 1957, Ray Lawler, Summer of the Seventeenth Doll, Sydney: Fontana Books, published 1974, page 68:
quote.text: The only time I walk out on singin' is when there's muckin' about and youse don't take it serious.
